summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a web-based space base game for kids ages 7 to 12, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
The goal: Keep 4 astronauts safe for 14 days on a Moon or Mars base.
How it works:
Each day you get ⚡ power from the Sun, and you share it between four machines: oxygen, greenhouse, radiation shield, and radio.
Every choice has a cost. Power given to one machine is power another one loses.
Sliders show simple cause-and-effect math, like "Oxygen −3 each day."
Surprise events such as solar flares, dust storms, and lunar nights test your planning.
The radio warns you about flares, but it costs power, and on Mars the messages are delayed by about 12 minutes.
What kids learn: Resource management, planning ahead, and real space facts about radiation, dust storms, and communication delays.
Tech: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with a Canvas-animated base that reacts to every decision. It works on phones and in light or dark mode.
details: PROJECT DETAILS: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a web game where kids run a Moon or Mars base for 14 days. Each day the player gets a limited amount of power, which depends on the weather (sunny day, lunar night, or Mars dust storm). They split it between four machines: the oxygen maker, greenhouse, radiation shield, and radio. Sliders show the result in simple math, like "Oxygen -3 each day." When the player ends the day, the base animation plays and a report explains what happened. Every choice costs something. The radio warns of solar flares, but it uses power the shield or greenhouse could have used. Unused power charges a battery for later. BENEFITS - Teaches resource management, trade-offs, and planning ahead - Introduces real space ideas: radiation, solar flares, dust storms, lunar nights, and communication delay - Gives instant visual feedback, so kids see cause and effect - Needs no install, account, or sign-up. It runs in any browser, including phones. INTENDED IMPACT We want kids aged 7 to 12 to feel that space exploration is something they can understand and be good at. We hope it sparks curiosity about STEM careers and shows that astronauts rely on careful planning as well as courage. TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY - HTML5, CSS, and JavaScript, with no frameworks - HTML Canvas 2D for the animated base - Google Fonts (Baloo 2 and Nunito) - Claude, an AI assistant, helped write and refine the code - No special hardware. A phone, tablet, or computer with a browser is enough. CREATIVITY - It is a living simulation, not a quiz or slideshow. - The base reacts visibly: plants grow, oxygen bubbles rise, radio waves pulse, and a shield bubble glows. - Solar flares appear as particles that bounce off the shield or break through. - Astronauts smile or frown based on crew health. - Players can't see a flare coming unless they pay for the radio, which turns the radio delay into a real choice. - Each daily report ends with a short space fact. FACTORS WE CONSIDERED - Age: Simple words, big sliders, bright colors, and gentle failure ("the crew flies home early") - Accessibility: Status uses text and symbols as well as color, and controls have clear focus outlines - Devices: Works on small screens and in light or dark mode - Science: Based on real facts, simplified for kids. For example, lunar night lasts about 14 Earth days, and Mars radio delay is shown as about 12 minutes - Balance: Two difficulty levels (Moon is easier, Mars is harder) and random events so every game feels different - Privacy: No accounts and no personal data collected
